segments.s107: What is CGPA, and how is it different from GPA and SGPA?
segments.s108: CGPA stands for Cumulative Grade Point Average. It is one number that sums up how you have performed across every semester you have completed so far. Universities print it on your transcript, employers ask for it on job applications, and scholarship committees use it to shortlist students. When someone says "my CGPA is 3.4", they mean their average for the whole degree up to now, not just the last semester.
segments.s109: The three terms sound alike, so here is the simple difference:
segments.s115: Your average for one semester (in some countries, for a year or the whole degree)
segments.s118: Your average for one semester. This is the name most Indian universities use, and it means the same as a semester GPA.
segments.s121: Your average across all the semesters you have completed
segments.s122: In short, SGPA and semester GPA describe one semester, while CGPA describes your whole journey. In the USA, "GPA" on its own often means the cumulative figure, which is why the words get mixed up. If a form asks about your degree as a whole, it almost always wants the cumulative number.
segments.s123: All three are weighted by credit hours. A 4-credit course affects your average more than a 1-credit lab, because it stands for more teaching time and more work.
segments.s124: How to calculate CGPA step by step
segments.s125: You don't need any special maths, just your grades and the credit hours of each course. This is the method most universities use:
segments.s126: Turn each grade into grade points. Use your university's grade point table (see the tables below). On the 4.0 scale, an A is usually 4.00 and a B+ is 3.33.
segments.s127: Multiply grade points by credit hours. This gives the "quality points" for each course. A 3-credit course with an A earns 3 × 4.00 = 12 quality points.
segments.s128: Work out the semester GPA. Add up the quality points for the semester and divide by the total credit hours. That is your semester GPA, or SGPA.
segments.s129: Combine your semesters. Multiply each semester's GPA by that semester's credit hours, add the results, and divide by the total credit hours of all semesters. The answer is your CGPA.
segments.s130: CGPA = Σ (semester GPA × semester credits) ÷ Σ (semester credits)

segments.s187: A CGPA can feel stuck, but it moves more than you might think, especially early in your degree. These habits make a real difference:
segments.s188: Focus on high-credit courses. A good grade in a 4-credit course lifts your CGPA more than the same grade in a 1-credit course, so plan your study time around that.
segments.s189: Don't ignore internal marks. Quizzes, assignments, labs and attendance often make up a big part of the final grade, and they are the easiest marks to secure.
segments.s190: Study a little every day. Reviewing your notes for 30 minutes after class works better than an all-night session before the exam, and you remember more.
segments.s191: Solve past papers. They show you the question style, the topics that come up most and how marks are awarded.
segments.s192: Ask for help early. Visit your teacher's office hours or ask a classmate in the week you get confused, not the week before finals.
segments.s193: Retake courses wisely. If your university replaces the old grade when you repeat a course, retaking a D or F can be one of the fastest ways to raise your CGPA.
segments.s194: Set a clear target. Use the Target tab to see exactly what GPA you need. "I need a 3.4 this semester" is much easier to act on than "I need to do better".
segments.s195: Look after yourself. Sleep, food and short breaks aren't wasted time. Tired students make careless mistakes in exams.
segments.s196: As your total credits grow, each new semester has a smaller effect on your CGPA. That means improving early is much easier than improving in your final year, so the best time to start is this semester.
segments.s198: Is CGPA the same as GPA?
segments.s199: Not exactly. GPA usually means your average for one semester, while CGPA is your average across all the semesters you have completed. In the USA, though, "GPA" on a transcript often means the cumulative figure. If a form asks for your GPA for the whole degree, give your CGPA.
segments.s200: How do I calculate CGPA from SGPA?
segments.s201: Multiply each semester's SGPA by that semester's credits, add the results, and divide by your total credits. If every semester has exactly the same number of credits, a simple average of your SGPAs gives the same answer.
segments.s202: Can I just average my semester GPAs?
segments.s203: Only when every semester has the same credit hours. Otherwise you need a credit-weighted average, because heavier semesters count for more. The CGPA tab of this calculator does this for you.
segments.s204: How do I convert CGPA to percentage?
segments.s205: On the 4.0 scale, divide your CGPA by 4 and multiply by 100. On the 10-point scale, the common method is CGPA × 9.5. Always check whether your university has its own official formula, because that is the one employers and admissions offices will use.
segments.s206: Why do we multiply by 9.5 for a 10-point CGPA?
segments.s207: CBSE introduced the 9.5 factor after comparing grade points with the marks students actually scored in past exams. Many Indian universities have adopted it, but not all of them, so check your university's rule.
segments.s209: On the 4.0 scale, 3.5 or above is generally seen as excellent and 3.0 or above as good. On the 10-point scale, 8.0 or above is strong and 7.0 or above is good. Cut-offs for jobs, scholarships and higher studies vary, so always check the exact requirement.
segments.s210: Can I raise my CGPA from 2.5 to 3.0?
segments.s211: Usually yes, if you have enough credits left. For example, with a 2.50 CGPA after 60 credits and 70 credits still to go, you need an average of about 3.43 in your remaining semesters. The Target tab of this calculator works this out for your own numbers.
segments.s212: Do failed or repeated courses count in CGPA?
segments.s213: It depends on your university. Many count an F as zero grade points until you pass the course. Some replace the old grade when you repeat a course, while others keep both grades in the average. Check your university's repeat policy.
segments.s214: How many decimal places should I write for my CGPA?
segments.s215: Most universities show CGPA to two decimal places, for example 3.37. On forms and CVs, write it exactly as it appears on your official transcript, and don't round it up yourself.
segments.s216: Is my data saved or shared anywhere?
segments.s217: Your entries are saved only in your own browser, so they are not lost when you refresh the page. Nothing is uploaded or shared. You can clear everything at any time with the Reset all button.
segments.s220: Results are estimates. Your university's official rules always come first.

segments.s233: CGPA Calculator: a result card showing a CGPA of 3.37 out of 4.00
segments.s235: Work out your semester GPA and overall CGPA with the official NUST undergraduate grade points (A = 4.00, B+ = 3.50, B = 3.00 and so on). How NUST grading works ↓
segments.s237: NUST uses relative grading, so enter the letter grade shown on your result. Grade points come from the NUST Undergraduate Student Handbook.
segments.s239: NUST uses relative grading: your grade depends on your class, not on fixed marks.
segments.s240: A minimum CGPA of 2.00 is needed to graduate (2.50 for BBA and some BS programmes).
segments.s241: If you repeat a course, only the better grade counts in your CGPA.
segments.s243: NUST uses relative grading on a 4.00 scale. In the words of the NUST Undergraduate Student Handbook, <q>The University follows a relative grading system on a scale of 1.00 to 4.00 points.</q> Your letter grade depends on how you performed compared with your class, not on a fixed percentage. An 82% could be an A in a tough paper and a B+ in an easier one.
segments.s244: Because of this, there is no reliable way to turn NUST marks straight into a grade, so this calculator asks for the letter grade on your result. Once you have your letters, the GPA maths is fixed and simple.
segments.s246: For a course with both theory and lab credits, NUST first combines the two percentages, weighted by credits, and then grades the course as a whole. The handbook's own example is Physics with 3 theory credits at 70% and 1 lab credit at 90%, which gives (70 × 3 + 90 × 1) ÷ 4 = 75%. You get one grade for all 4 credits, so enter it in the calculator as one 4-credit subject.
segments.s251: Undergraduate only; the lowest grade that earns course credits
segments.s252: F because of a shortage of attendance
segments.s253: I (incomplete), W (dropped), Q (qualified) and T (transfer) carry no grade points. Notice that NUST has no A+ and no minus grades: B+ and C+ sit half a point above B and C.
segments.s254: How to calculate your NUST GPA: worked example
segments.s260: Your CGPA works the same way across all semesters: add up the credits × points for every course you have taken and divide by your total credit hours. The CGPA tab does this from your semester GPAs.
segments.s261: Minimum CGPA and academic deficiency at NUST
segments.s262: To graduate you need a minimum CGPA of 2.00, or 2.50 for BBA, BS Economics, BS Public Administration, BS Mass Communication, BS Accounting & Finance and BS Psychology.
segments.s263: BE and BS students also need at least a C in their final-year (design) project, where applicable.
segments.s264: You are academically deficient if you get an F or XF in any course, a semester GPA below 2.00, a CGPA below 2.00, an I (incomplete) grade, or less than a C in your final-year project.
segments.s265: If your CGPA has dropped below 2.00, the Target tab shows the GPA you need in your remaining semesters to get back above it.
segments.s266: Repeating a course to improve your CGPA
segments.s267: When you repeat a course, your transcript shows both the old and the new grade, but only the better grade is used to compute your CGPA. Repeating needs permission from your HoD, and grades earned by repeating don't count towards top academic honours and awards, except the Rector's Gold Medal. If you fail a course again after repeating it, it still counts as one F.
segments.s268: Calculator tip: for a repeated course, enter only the better grade.
segments.s270: The NUST Undergraduate Student Handbook does not include an official formula for converting CGPA into a percentage. When a percentage is needed, many people use (CGPA ÷ 4) × 100, so 3.40 becomes 85%. Employers and universities sometimes use their own rules, so check what the organisation you're applying to accepts. The Percentage tab uses this simple method.
segments.s272: Does NUST use relative or absolute grading?
segments.s273: NUST uses relative grading on a 4.00 scale, so your grade depends on your performance compared with your class rather than on a fixed percentage. That is why there is no fixed marks-to-grade table for NUST.
segments.s274: What are the grade points for each grade at NUST?
segments.s275: A is 4.00, B+ is 3.50, B is 3.00, C+ is 2.50, C is 2.00, D+ is 1.50 and D is 1.00. F and XF (F because of a shortage of attendance) are 0.00. D+ and D are used for undergraduate students only.
segments.s276: Is there an A+ or A- grade at NUST?
segments.s277: No. A (4.00) is the highest grade and there are no minus grades. B+ and C+ sit half a point above B and C.
segments.s278: What CGPA do I need to graduate from NUST?
segments.s279: A minimum CGPA of 2.00, or 2.50 for BBA, BS Economics, BS Public Administration, BS Mass Communication, BS Accounting & Finance and BS Psychology. BE and BS students also need at least a C in their final-year project where applicable.
segments.s280: If I repeat a course at NUST, which grade counts?
segments.s281: Your transcript shows both grades, but only the better grade is used in your CGPA. Grades earned by repeating do not count towards top academic awards, except the Rector’s Gold Medal.
segments.s282: How do I convert my NUST CGPA to a percentage?
segments.s283: The NUST undergraduate handbook does not give an official formula. The common method is (CGPA ÷ 4) × 100, so 3.40 becomes 85%, but check what the employer or university you are applying to accepts.
segments.s284: How do I enter a course that has a lab?
segments.s285: Enter it as one subject with its total credit hours, for example 4 for a 3+1 course. NUST combines the theory and lab marks into one grade for the whole course.

segments.s318: COMSATS CGPA to percentage: the official rule
segments.s319: COMSATS does not use (CGPA ÷ 4) × 100. Its notification says: <q>A student getting any CGPA will be given the minimum of the corresponding percentage… For example, if a student gets a CGPA of 3.00, the percentage associated will be 71%.</q>
segments.s320: In plain words, find the band your CGPA falls in. Your percentage is the lowest percentage of that band.
segments.s321: For example, a CGPA of 3.39 is in the A- band (3.34–3.66), so it counts as 80%. The simple formula would give 84.75%, almost 5 points higher, which could cause problems if an employer checks with the university.
segments.s323: The notification covers students admitted from Fall 2021. If you joined COMSATS earlier, your transcript may follow the older COMSATS grading scheme. The GPA and CGPA maths (a credit-weighted average) is the same, but the grade bands and the percentage rule may be different, so check your transcript or ask your campus examination office.
segments.s325: Why does COMSATS give a range of grade points for each grade?
segments.s326: Since Fall 2021, COMSATS follows the HEC grading criteria, where each letter grade covers a range of grade points. Your exact points depend on your marks, so two students with an A- can have different grade points.
segments.s327: How do I convert my COMSATS CGPA to a percentage?
segments.s328: Find the band your CGPA falls in and take the lowest percentage of that band. For example, 3.40 is in the A- band (3.34 to 3.66), so it equals 80%. The Percentage tab does this for you.
segments.s329: What percentage is a 3.00 CGPA at COMSATS?
segments.s330: It is 71%. This exact example is given in the COMSATS notification: a 3.00 CGPA falls in the B band (2.67 to 3.00), whose lowest percentage is 71%.
segments.s331: Can I use CGPA × 25 or (CGPA ÷ 4) × 100 for COMSATS?
segments.s332: Not for students admitted from Fall 2021. Those formulas usually give a higher number than the official COMSATS rule, which uses the lowest percentage of the band your CGPA falls in.
segments.s333: What are the passing marks at COMSATS?
segments.s334: In the Fall 2021 grading table, 50% to 53% is a D, and anything below 50% is an F with 0.00 grade points.
segments.s335: Can I use this calculator if I was admitted before Fall 2021?
segments.s336: The GPA and CGPA maths is the same for everyone, so you can still enter your grade points. But the grade bands and the percentage rule on this page apply to Fall 2021 admissions onward, so check your transcript if you joined earlier.

segments.s353: Which VTU scheme are you in?
segments.s354: VTU updates its regulations from time to time. The Regulations 2022 apply to students admitted from the 2022-23 academic year onwards, while the 2021 regulations took effect from 2021-22. Choose your scheme at the top of the calculator, because the grade letters and the CGPA-to-percentage formula are different.
segments.s356: VTU uses absolute grading. Your marks in CIE (continuous internal evaluation) and SEE (semester end examination) are added and turned into a percentage, and that percentage decides your grade (clause 22OB 6.1).
segments.s360: How VTU calculates SGPA and CGPA
segments.s361: SGPA = Σ (Ci × Gi) ÷ Σ Ci    CGPA = Σ (Ci × Si) ÷ Σ Ci
segments.s362: Ci is a course's credits and Gi its grade point. For CGPA, Si is each semester's SGPA and Ci that semester's total credits. Both are rounded to 2 decimal places (clause 22OB 6.6). Here is a 2022-scheme example:
segments.s374: 2022 scheme: Percentage = CGPA × 10, so a CGPA of 8.20 becomes 82% (clause 22OB 6.7). The regulation says this formula may be used for employment and higher studies.
segments.s375: 2021 scheme and the 2015 CBCS scheme: Percentage = (CGPA − 0.75) × 10, so the same 8.20 becomes 74.5%. That is why you will find two different VTU formulas online: each is correct for its own scheme. If you are on the 2017 or 2018 scheme, check the formula printed in your regulations or on your grade card.
segments.s377: First Class with Distinction: 70% or more, a CGPA of 7.00 and above
segments.s378: First Class: 60% to below 70%, a CGPA from 6.00 to 6.99
segments.s379: Second Class: 50% to below 60%, a CGPA from 5.00 to 5.99
segments.s380: Pass Class: 40% to 50%, a CGPA from 4.00 to 4.99
segments.s382: CIE is worth up to 50 marks, and you need at least 40% of the CIE maximum to be allowed to sit the SEE.
segments.s383: In the SEE, also worth up to 50 marks, you need at least 35% of the maximum.
segments.s384: Overall you need at least 40% in the course, which is a P grade.
segments.s385: To pass the whole programme, you need a P grade or better in every registered course.
segments.s387: How do I convert VTU CGPA to percentage?
segments.s388: For the 2022 scheme, multiply your CGPA by 10, so 8.20 becomes 82%. For the 2021 scheme and the older 2015 CBCS scheme, use (CGPA − 0.75) × 10, so 8.20 becomes 74.5%.
segments.s389: Why do some websites say to subtract 0.75 from VTU CGPA?
segments.s390: Older VTU regulations, including the 2015 CBCS and 2021-22 regulations, used (CGPA − 0.75) × 10. The 2022 regulations changed it to CGPA × 10. Each formula is correct for its own scheme.
segments.s391: What CGPA do I need for First Class with Distinction in VTU?
segments.s392: Under the 2022 scheme, First Class with Distinction needs 70% or more, which means a CGPA of at least 7.00. First Class is 60% to below 70%, which is a CGPA from 6.00 to 6.99.
segments.s393: What are the passing marks in the VTU 2022 scheme?
segments.s394: You need at least 40% of the CIE marks to sit the SEE, at least 35% of the SEE marks, and at least 40% overall in the course, which is a P grade.
segments.s395: Is VTU grading relative or absolute?
segments.s396: Absolute. Your CIE and SEE marks are added and turned into a percentage, and fixed ranges decide your grade, for example 90 to 100 for an O in the 2022 scheme.
segments.s397: How is CGPA calculated from SGPA in VTU?
segments.s398: Multiply each semester’s SGPA by that semester’s total credits, add the results and divide by the total credits of all semesters. SGPA and CGPA are rounded to 2 decimal places.

segments.s408: Almost every student has sat with a transcript and a phone calculator, trying to work out their GPA before results come out or wondering what they need next semester to reach a goal. The maths isn't hard, but it's easy to slip up: forgetting to weight by credit hours, using the wrong grade points, or applying the wrong percentage formula.
segments.s409: CGPA Calculator takes that stress away. You type in your subjects or semesters and the answer appears straight away. We also show the formula, so you can see exactly how each number was worked out.

segments.s423: We use the most common grading tables and formulas, and we test our calculations carefully. segments.s428: How CGPA Calculator handles your data: your grades stay in your browser. Also explains how analytics and ads may use cookies in future.
segments.s430: The short version: the numbers you type stay on your own device. You don't need an account, and we don't collect your grades.
segments.s433: Your grades, marks and GPAs are worked out in your browser and never sent to us.
segments.s434: We don't currently use analytics, advertising or cookies of our own.
segments.s435: We may add Google Analytics and ads (such as Google AdSense) in future. This page explains what that would mean, and we will update it before either goes live.
segments.s436: 1. Information you enter in the calculator
segments.s437: Everything you type into the calculator, such as subject names, credit hours, grades, marks and GPAs, is processed entirely in your web browser. It is saved in your browser's local storage so your entries are still there when you come back, and it is never sent to us or to anyone else.
segments.s438: You can delete this information at any time with the Reset all button on the calculator, or by clearing your browser's data for this site.
segments.s440: Like almost every website, the service that hosts this site may automatically record basic technical information when you visit. This can include your IP address, browser and device type, the pages you request, and the date and time of your visit. This information is used to deliver the site and keep it secure, and is handled under the hosting provider's own privacy policy.
segments.s442: At the moment, this website does not set any cookies of its own. It uses your browser's local storage only to remember your calculator entries and whether you prefer light or dark mode. This information stays on your device.
segments.s443: If we add analytics or advertising in future, cookies may be used as described in the next two sections.
segments.s445: In future we may use Google Analytics, a web analytics service provided by Google, to understand how visitors use the site, for example which tools are most popular and which devices people use. This helps us improve the calculator. If we do:
segments.s446: Google Analytics will use cookies and similar technologies to collect information such as the pages you visit, how long you stay, your approximate location (city or country), your device and browser type, and how you found the site.
segments.s447: This information will be processed by Google in line with the Google Privacy Policy. You can read how Google uses information from sites that use its services.
segments.s448: We will not send Google the grades or numbers you type into the calculator, and we will not use analytics to identify you personally.
segments.s449: You can opt out of Google Analytics on all websites by installing the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on.
segments.s451: To keep the calculator free, we may show ads in future, for example through Google AdSense. If we do:
segments.s452: Third-party vendors, including Google, will use cookies to serve ads based on your previous visits to this website or other websites.
segments.s453: Google's use of advertising cookies lets Google and its partners show you ads based on your visits to this site and/or other sites on the internet.
segments.s454: You can opt out of personalised advertising in Google's My Ad Center (formerly Ads Settings). You can also opt out of some other vendors' personalised ads at optout.aboutads.info, or at youronlinechoices.eu if you are in Europe.
segments.s455: Ads will always be kept separate from the calculator, and advertisers will never receive the numbers you enter.
segments.s457: If you visit from a place where the law requires your consent before analytics or advertising cookies are used, such as the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom, we will ask for your consent with a cookie notice before any such cookies are set. You can change your mind at any time.
segments.s458: You can also block or delete cookies in your browser settings, or use a private browsing window. The calculator will keep working, although your entries won't be remembered after you close the window.
segments.s460: This website is meant for students and is suitable for a general audience. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13. If you believe a child has sent us personal information, for example by email, please contact us and we will delete it.
segments.s462: If you contact us by email, we will receive your email address and anything you include in your message. We use this only to reply to you, and we do not sell or share it. Please don't send transcripts, ID documents or other sensitive information.
segments.s464: This site may link to other websites, such as Google's privacy pages. We are not responsible for the content or privacy practices of those websites, so please read their policies too.
segments.s466: We may update this policy from time to time, for example when we add analytics or advertising. We will change the "Last updated" date at the top of this page, and we will update this policy before any new kind of data collection begins.
segments.s468: If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy, please get in touch through our Contact page.
segments.s470: The terms for using CGPA Calculator, including our disclaimer: always confirm results with your university's official grading rules.
segments.s471: By using this website, you agree to these terms. We have kept them short and written them in plain language.
segments.s473: CGPA Calculator gives estimates for guidance only. Grading scales, grade point values, rounding rules and CGPA-to-percentage formulas differ between universities, boards and countries. Always confirm your results with your own university's official rules, transcript or examination office before you use them in an application, a form or any important decision.
segments.s475: CGPA Calculator is a free website that helps students estimate their semester GPA, overall CGPA, target CGPA and CGPA-to-percentage conversion. You don't need an account to use it.
segments.s477: You may use the website for personal, educational and non-commercial purposes. When using it, please don't:
segments.s478: try to disrupt, damage or overload the website, or access it in ways it was not designed for;
segments.s479: copy or republish large parts of the website, its content or its code as your own;
segments.s480: present results from this website as an official university document or record, or use them to misrepresent your grades.
segments.s482: We work hard to keep our formulas and grade tables accurate, but we cannot guarantee that the results will match your university's official figures. Your results also depend on the information you enter, so a typing mistake will lead to a wrong answer.
segments.s483: If there is any difference between a result on this website and your university's official records, your university's records are always correct. CGPA Calculator is an independent website and is not connected with, or approved by, any university, examination board or education authority.
segments.s485: The website is provided "as is" and "as available". We do not promise that it will always be available, error-free or suitable for any particular purpose, and we may change or remove features at any time.
segments.s487: To the fullest extent allowed by law, we are not responsible for any loss or damage that results from using, or not being able to use, this website. This includes decisions about admissions, scholarships, jobs, visas or course choices that were based on results from this website.

segments.s490: 7. Advertising and links to other websites
segments.s491: The website may show advertisements in future and may link to other websites. We are not responsible for the content, products or services of advertisers or other websites, and a link or advertisement does not mean we recommend them.
segments.s493: The design, text, graphics and code of this website belong to CGPA Calculator. You are welcome to share links to the website and to use your own results for personal purposes.
segments.s495: We may update these terms from time to time. When we do, we will change the "Last updated" date at the top of this page. If you keep using the website after a change, you accept the updated terms.
segments.s497: If you have any questions about these terms, please get in touch through our Contact page.
segments.s499: Questions, feedback or found a mistake? Email the CGPA Calculator team. You can also ask us to add your university's grading scale.
